summary: This experimental memo defines how to use Kerberos Version 4 to authenticate a user within the Telnet authentication option. It is one of several authentication types Telnet could negotiate.

plainLanguage.summary: Kerberos is like a ticket booth that gives you a pass proving who you are. This paper explains how to show that pass when logging into a remote computer.

questions: how does telnet kerberos mutual authentication work
subtitle: Use Kerberos Version 4 to authenticate users in Telnet sessions.

tldr.problem: Telnet needed a way to authenticate users securely without transmitting passwords in the clear, and Kerberos Version 4 was an existing authentication system available for this purpose.
tldr.mechanism: Telnet's authentication option can negotiate Kerberos V4 as an authentication mechanism, allowing the client to send a Kerberos ticket, which the server validates. Mutual authentication is optional via a challenge-response exchange.
tldr.outcome: Systems using Kerberos V4 can authenticate Telnet sessions, with optional mutual authentication to verify the server identity.

today: RFC 1411 is an Experimental Internet Standard. Kerberos V4 is largely superseded by Kerberos V5, and modern systems typically use Kerberos V5 or other authentication mechanisms like public key authentication instead of Telnet with Kerberos V4.

sections.title: Kerberos V4 Authentication for Telnet
sections.content: Telnet is a protocol for remote login sessions, and it includes an Authentication option that allows client and server to negotiate a common authentication mechanism. This document specifies how Kerberos Version 4 can be used as one such mechanism. The authentication type is identified as KERBEROS_V4 (code 1). The mechanism uses Kerberos tickets and an optional mutual authentication exchange to prove the identity of both the client and server. The authenticator used is a Kerberos principal of the form rcmd.host@realm, following the convention for Kerberos service principals.
sections.plainLanguage: Remote login (Telnet) can use Kerberos to check who you are before letting you in. The server asks for your Kerberos ticket, and if it is real, you get access.

sections.title: The Authentication Exchange
sections.content: The Kerberos V4 authentication in Telnet uses several suboption commands: AUTH transmits the Kerberos ticket to the remote side; ACCEPT indicates successful authentication; REJECT indicates failure (optionally with a reason message); and CHALLENGE and RESPONSE are used for mutual authentication. When mutual authentication is negotiated (AUTH_HOW_MUTUAL bit set), after successful initial authentication, the client sends an encrypted 8-byte challenge, the server decrypts and increments it, re-encrypts and returns it, and the client verifies the response. This challenge is also used as a seed to generate a default encryption key for the Encryption option.
sections.plainLanguage: First, the client sends its ticket. The server checks it and says accept or reject. If they both want to check each other, they send encrypted numbers back and forth to make sure they are really talking to each other.

sections.title: How It Works in Practice
sections.content: The protocol supports two authentication directions. If the client-to-server bit is set, the client sends the initial AUTH command, and the server responds with ACCEPT or REJECT. If the server-to-client bit is set, the direction is reversed. The mutual authentication bits control whether an additional challenge-response exchange occurs after initial authentication succeeds. A user can log in as a different username by first sending a NAME command with the desired username, allowing the server to grant access to that account if the authenticated user is authorized.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends a ticket for user X, and the server can decide to let user X log in as a different user Y if that is allowed. They can also check that they are really talking to each other by passing secret numbers back and forth.

references.text: Ylonen, T. and C. Lonvick, Ed., "The Secure Shell (SSH) Transport Layer Protocol", RFC 4253, January 2006.
